title: Fast Thinking, Slow Thinking
objective: After this level you can explain the two-systems idea of fast intuition and slow deliberation, and when each takes over.
summary: Psychologists describe a fast, automatic System 1 and a slow, deliberate System 2. The bat-and-ball puzzle shows how often the quick answer goes out unchecked.

cards.headline: A bat and a ball cost $1.10. The bat costs $1 more. What's the ball?
cards.body: Most people have an answer before they finish reading the question. Hold on to yours. This level is about where it came from, and why it is so often wrong.

cards.headline: Two ways of thinking
cards.body: Psychologists describe two modes of thought, which Keith Stanovich and Richard West labeled System 1 and System 2 in 2000. System 1 is fast, automatic, effortless and hard to control; it works much like perception, handing you answers you never asked for. System 2 is slower, effortful and deliberate. Most everyday judgments come from System 1, but System 2 can modify or override them. Daniel Kahneman, who shared the 2002 Nobel Prize in economics, built his account of judgment on this split.

cards.headline: The checker that barely checks
cards.body: The answer that pops up is 10 cents: $1.10 splits neatly into $1 and 10 cents, and 10 cents feels about right for a ball. Check it, though: the bat has to cost a whole dollar more than the ball. The ball costs 5 cents. Shane Frederick found that 50 percent of Princeton students and 56 percent at the University of Michigan gave the wrong answer. System 2 is supposed to monitor System 1, but its monitoring is normally quite lax.

mascot.line: Keep this one: fast answers aren't the problem. Unchecked fast answers are.

cards.headline: A test for the checker
cards.body: In 2005 Frederick turned the puzzle into one item of a three-item Cognitive Reflection Test. It measures the ability or disposition to reflect on a question and resist the first response that comes to mind. Scores relate to real choices about time and risk: people who go with the quick answer on such puzzles tend to be less patient about waiting for delayed rewards.

cards.headline: Fast and slow thinking
learned: The bat and ball: the quick answer goes unchecked

questions.prompt: In the two-systems idea, which description fits System 1?

options.label: Used only for doing arithmetic
options.rationale: System 1 produces most everyday judgments, not just sums.

options.label: A brain region seen on scans
options.rationale: The systems describe modes of thinking, not a place in the brain.

questions.explanation: System 1 is fast, automatic, effortless and hard to control. System 2 is the slower, deliberate one.

questions.prompt: Why did about half of Frederick's Princeton students get the bat-and-ball puzzle wrong?

options.label: The puzzle has no single right answer
options.rationale: It does: the ball costs 5 cents.

options.label: The arithmetic was too hard for them
options.rationale: The math is easy once you check the tempting answer.

options.label: Their quick answer went out unchecked
They misread the price of the ball
options.rationale: The trap is the neat split of $1.10, not a misreading.

questions.explanation: The intuitive answer, 10 cents, arrives fast, and System 2's monitoring is normally lax, so many people report it without checking.

questions.prompt: System 1 and System 2 describe what goes on inside the mind. The Level 6 shift that brought the mind back as something science could study was _____.

options.label: behaviorism
options.rationale: Behaviorism set the mind aside and studied only behavior.

options.label: introspection
options.rationale: That was Wundt's method of looking inward, from Level 3.

options.label: psychoanalysis
options.rationale: That was Freud's approach, from Level 4.

questions.explanation: By the 1950s the cognitive revolution revived interest in the mind as a subject of science.
